1.name: Drive-end frame
1.spec: Cast housing with the 6203 bearing's boss
1.note: Carries the front bearing and the belt's pull, and clamps the stator to the rear frame. Air from the fan behind the pulley is drawn through it.

2.name: Slip-ring-end frame and brush holder
2.spec: Rear housing, 6201 bearing, moulded brush holder
2.note: Holds the rear bearing, the two brushes over the slip rings and the rectifier; it is itself the heat sink of the three negative diodes.

3.name: Stator
3.note: Stands still. Each claw passing a slot drives its coil's current one way and the next claw the other, so the three phases carry AC, 120° apart.

4.name: Claw-pole rotor and shaft
4.spec: Two 7-claw halves on a core, 14 poles
4.note: One coil, fourteen poles: the field winding magnetises the core, so every claw of the front half is a north pole and every claw of the rear half a south.

5.name: Field winding
5.spec: On a nylon bobbin between the pole halves, 8.4 Ω hot
5.note: Up to 3.3 A at 28 V. The regulator controls the alternator by this current alone: a few amps here switch the 60 A output.

6.name: Slip rings
6.spec: Two rings Ø23 on a phenolic sleeve
6.note: Carry the field current into the turning rotor. Unlike a commutator they never switch it: the field is DC, only the stator's current alternates.

7.name: Brushes and springs
7.note: Slide on the slip rings. They carry only the field's few amps, so they last; worn short, the field opens and the alternator stops charging.

8.name: Rectifier
8.spec: Six diodes in two heat sinks, B+ stud M6
8.note: A three-phase bridge: three diodes let each phase push current out to B+, three let it return from ground, and none lets the battery back into the stator.

9.name: Pulley and fan
9.note: Three times smaller than the crank's pulley, so the alternator turns at three times engine speed: 2,100 rpm at idle, 7,350 in cruise.

10.name: Ball bearings
10.note: The front one takes the belt's pull; the smaller rear one sits beyond the slip rings in the rear frame.

11.name: Alternator V-belt
11.spec: Single V in the crank's and the alternator's pulleys
11.note: The one link between the engine and the alternator. On the tour it breaks: the alternator stops and everything electrical runs from the battery.

12.name: Voltage regulator
12.spec: 28.0 V, switching the field's ground, overvoltage relay
12.note: Senses the bus and switches the field on and off thousands of times a second: the longer it is on, the higher the field current and the output.

13.name: Battery case, lid and vent caps
13.spec: Two rows of six cells, 160 × 180 × 190 overall
13.note: Holds twelve cells in two rows; vented caps let the gas of charging out. It sits in a vented box ahead of the firewall.

14.name: Cell elements and electrolyte
14.spec: 4 positive, 5 negative plates a cell, SG 1.11–1.285
14.note: Each cell makes SG + 0.84 V, 2.12 V full. Discharge turns both plates to lead sulphate and the acid toward water, so its gravity tells the charge.

15.name: Battery contactor
15.spec: Continuous-duty relay, coil grounded by the BAT switch
15.note: A heavy relay at the battery: the master switch carries only its coil's half amp, so no heavy cable has to run to the panel.

16.name: Starter contactor
16.spec: Intermittent-duty relay, coil from the key's START
16.note: Closes for as long as the key is held at START and puts the battery straight onto the starter: 330 A at the first instant, about 130 A cranking.

17.name: Split master switch
17.spec: ALT and BAT rockers, ALT interlocked to BAT
17.note: BAT closes the battery contactor; ALT feeds the regulator, so the field. ALT can be switched off alone, to shed the field after a failure.

18.name: Starter frames, magnets and brushes
18.spec: Yoke Ø76 with ferrite magnets, drive and commutator end frames
18.note: A direct-drive permanent-magnet DC motor: its stall current is limited only by the battery, the cables and its own 50 mΩ.

19.name: Starter armature and commutator
19.spec: Laminated, lap-wound, on the drive's shaft
19.note: Turns at about 2,400 rpm cranking, 13.5 times the crank. As it speeds up its back-EMF grows and the current falls from the inrush.

20.name: Bendix drive and pinion
20.spec: 11-tooth pinion on a 64 mm-lead helical screw, drive spring
20.note: As the armature spins up the pinion's inertia holds it back, so it screws 16 mm along the helix into the ring gear; once the engine fires, it is thrown out.

21.name: Main bus bar
21.note: Every source feeds it and every breaker draws from it. Its voltage is whatever balances them: 28 V with the alternator on line, the battery's own below that.

22.name: Avionics master switch and bus
22.spec: Rocker, feeding the avionics bus through a 15 A breaker
22.note: Off for engine start, so the radios never see the starter's sag; on, it feeds every radio's own breaker.

23.name: Ammeter and shunt
23.spec: Centre-zero ±60 A, 50 mV shunt in the battery lead
23.note: Reads the battery's current: + while the alternator charges it, − while it feeds the bus. The starter is tapped off before the shunt, so it never shows.

24.name: Low-voltage annunciator
24.spec: On below 24.5 V, off above 25.0 V
24.note: On whenever the bus is below what the alternator would hold: while cranking, before it comes on line, and when it fails. The pilot's first warning.

25.name: Circuit breaker
25.note: A bimetal carries the circuit's current and bends as it heats; past 125 % of its rating it unlatches the button, which pops out showing a white band.
